title: Sleep or journey
hook: Socrates, just sentenced to death: it is either a dreamless sleep or a journey, and neither is to be feared

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ecclesiastes: a time to be born, and a time to die. Your line was what I think now, your own voice before the teachers'.

The vote has just been counted. An Athenian jury has sentenced an old man to death for corrupting the young and failing to honor the city's gods. A person might rage, or beg, or go silent. Socrates turns to the jurors who voted to acquit him and says, in effect: stay a minute, friends, let's talk while the officials are busy. And what he wants to talk about is the thing just handed to him. In Plato's account of the trial, the Apology, he lays out two possibilities for what death is, two doors, and walks through neither.
screen: `THE VERDICT IS IN.` → `STAY A MINUTE, FRIENDS.` → `TWO POSSIBILITIES.`

segments.voice: First, a silence he trusts. Socrates says an inner sign has all his life stopped him when he was about to do wrong, even in small things. That day it never stopped him: not leaving home, not walking into court, not in his speech. He takes its silence as a hint that what is happening may be good. Second, the first door: sleep. Maybe death is nothing at all, no awareness, like a night of sleep without even a dream. Think of your best night of deep sleep, he tells the jurors, and set it against all the other days and nights of your life. Even the great king of Persia, he says, would find few days and nights better. If death is like that, he says, it is a gain. Third, the second door: a journey. Maybe death is a move to another place, where the dead are. Then he would meet the poets and heroes of old and keep asking questions, testing who is wise. And there, he jokes, they surely don't put you to death for asking. Fourth, either way. Socrates doesn't claim to know which door is real. His point is that neither gives a reason to be afraid. He tells them a good person has nothing evil to fear, in life or after death. And he ends: now it's time to go, I to die and you to live, and which of us goes to the better thing, only God knows. That is Plato's Socrates. Others in this block will answer differently, on their own days.
screen: `THE SIGN THAT STAYED SILENT.` · `DOOR ONE: A DREAMLESS SLEEP.` · `DOOR TWO: A JOURNEY.` · `NEITHER IS TO BE FEARED.` · then, large: `EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Take the first door: think of the deepest sleep you can remember, the kind where no time seemed to pass, and rest there a few breaths. Then take the second: a long trip, a new place, people you've wanted to meet, and rest there too. Hold both without choosing, and notice whether fear shows up in either; if this is tender today, rest in the breath instead.
Hypnos, Socrates's first picture of death in Plato's Apology: a sleep with no dream, no cause for fear. Today's word.
Your line: either way. Two doors, and fear behind neither. Day seven hundred sixty, done.

howItsDone: Students of philosophy read Socrates's closing words in Plato's Apology as an example of facing death with reasoning rather than fear, without claiming to know what death is.

chat.says: How could Socrates stay calm right after being sentenced to death?
options: He saw two possibilities, dreamless sleep or a journey, and feared neither.
He was sure the jury would change its mind before the day was out.
He was planning to escape Athens with his friends that same night.
